subject: PSHE
board: PSHE Association / statutory Relationships and Health Education guidance
source: National Curriculum / statutory guidance (Relationships Education and Health Education only); PSHE Association programme of study themes; TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27 and TGA RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y1-Y2 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly. No RSE or sex education in Years 1 to 6 (owner decision, October 2026): body-safety safeguarding only, taught at a non-sexual level.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Relationships and the online world
lessons.title: Peer pressure: being true to yourself
objectives: Define peer pressure and recognise it
Use assertive responses to say no
Link integrity and truthfulness to making good choices

keywords.def: influence from people your age to do something
calm, firm and respectful
doing the right thing even when no one is watching
the power to affect what someone thinks or does
what happens as a result of a choice

starter: Bismillah. Name two ways to be a good friend.

teach.heading: What is peer pressure?
bullets: Pressure from friends or groups
Can be spoken or unspoken
Can be positive or negative
Examples: dares, trends, being left out
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain peer pressure with relatable invented examples: copying a trend, joining a joke at someone's expense, trying a dare. Ask: ‘Can peer pressure ever be positive?’ (yes, such as a friend encouraging you to study or pray). Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Why do we go along?
bullets: Want to fit in
Fear of being left out
Fear of being laughed at
It feels hard to say no
teach.note: Normalise these feelings: wanting friends is natural. Ask: ‘What is the worst that could happen if you say no?’ Compare with what could happen if you say yes to something wrong. Link to the hadith of the Prophet (peace be upon him) that a person is on the way of life of his close friend, so look carefully at who you take as friends (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi).

teach.heading: Assertive responses
bullets: Say no clearly: ‘No, thanks.’
Give a reason if you want
Suggest something else
Walk away or tell an adult
teach.note: Model three styles: passive (mumbling), aggressive (shouting), assertive (calm and firm). Practise short phrases: ‘That’s not for me.’ ‘I’m going to head off now.’ Ask pupils to identify which style is most effective and respectful. Make sure they know that saying no is a sign of strength.

teach.heading: Integrity in action
bullets: Truthfulness: do the right thing alone
Think: would Allah be pleased?
Choose friends who support good choices
Qur'an 9:119: be with the truthful
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 9:119 tells believers to be mindful of Allah and be with the truthful. Discuss how our values help us decide. Ask: ‘Who helps you be your best self?’ Link to RECIPE Integrity.

practice: Passive, aggressive or assertive? (a) ‘Fine, whatever, I’ll do it.’ (b) ‘Don’t be stupid!’ (c) ‘No thanks, I’m not doing that.’
A friend asks you to copy their homework. Write an assertive response and an alternative suggestion.
Name two positive peer influences in your life.
independent: Role-play with a partner: one persuades, one responds assertively. Use three different scenarios.
Write a short advice card: ‘How to say no kindly’ with three phrases.
Explain in four sentences how your values help you resist pressure.
exit: Define peer pressure and give one example.
Give one assertive way to say no.
lessons.homework: Interview a trusted adult about a time they had to say no under pressure and write four sentences about what they did.
lessons.send: SEND: provide response cards and visuals for the three styles. EAL: model phrases and allow rehearsal. Stretch: create a short comic strip showing peer pressure and a positive response.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Relationships and the online world
lessons.title: Online life: digital footprints, trust and reporting
objectives: Explain what a digital footprint is and how it lasts
Judge whether online information is reliable

keywords.def: the trail of information about you that stays online
able to be trusted
where information comes from
false or misleading information
to tell a trusted adult or the platform about a concern

starter: Name one piece of private information.

teach.heading: Your digital footprint
bullets: Everything you post leaves a trail
Photos, comments and likes can be copied
Once online, it can be hard to remove
Future teachers or employers may see it
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain digital footprints with the idea of footprints in wet sand that someone could follow, or ones that stay like concrete. Ask: ‘What would you like your footprint to say about you?’ Remind pupils that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to speak good or remain silent (Bukhari and Muslim); this applies to typing as well as speaking. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Think before you post
bullets: Is it kind and true?
Would I be happy if my family saw it?
Does it share someone's private information?
Ask permission before sharing photos of others
teach.note: Teach the pause-and-check habit. Give invented examples: sharing a classmate's photo, posting while angry, replying to a rude comment. Link to privacy and respect. Remind pupils that many social media platforms set a minimum age of 13.

teach.heading: Can we trust it?
bullets: Check who made it
Look for other sources
Beware of shocking headlines
Ask an adult if unsure
teach.note: Show an invented example of a dramatic but false headline. Ask: ‘How can we check?’ Teach three checks: Who wrote it? When? What do other trusted sources say? Connect to the Qur'an's guidance to verify news before acting on it (49:6). Explain that misinformation spreads fast.

teach.heading: When something goes wrong
bullets: Tell a trusted adult
Block and report in the app
CEOP Safety Centre for online abuse
Childline: 0800 1111
teach.note: Give clear steps. Reassure pupils that anyone can make a mistake online and help is available without blame. Mention that sharing someone's private or inappropriate images is serious and must be reported. If a pupil discloses a safeguarding concern, follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

practice: Would you post it? (a) A photo of your class trip with names. (b) A kind comment on a friend's drawing. (c) An angry message about a classmate.
Use the three checks on this headline: ‘Scientists say sleep is bad for you!’ What would you do next?
Name two places you can report a concern.
independent: Create a ‘Think before you post’ checklist with five questions.
Write four sentences about the kind of digital footprint you want to leave.
Write a short message to a friend who has shared something they regret, offering advice.
exit: Name one way to check if information is reliable.
lessons.homework: With a parent or carer, review your device settings and write down two privacy settings you can change.
lessons.send: SEND: provide checklist cards and picture prompts. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: research an example of misinformation and how it was corrected.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Healthy mind and growing up
lessons.title: Looking after our mental wellbeing: stress, balance and support
objectives: Explain that mental health is as important as physical health
Identify things that cause stress and ways to cope

keywords.def: how we think, feel and cope
a feeling of being under pressure
being healthy, happy and comfortable
something you do to manage a hard feeling
help from other people

starter: Name two ways to say no assertively.

teach.heading: Mind and body
bullets: Mental health is part of health
Everyone has ups and downs
Good mental health helps us learn and enjoy life
It is okay to need support
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain that looking after our minds is as important as looking after our bodies. Ask pupils to rate their mood privately on a 1-5 scale and not to share unless they wish. Cite plainly: Qur'an 13:28 teaches that hearts find rest in remembering Allah. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: What causes stress?
bullets: Tests and homework
Friendship problems
Changes at home or school
Too much screen time or news
teach.note: Ask pupils to suggest causes of stress without personal details. Make a class list. Normalise: stress is a natural response; a little can help us focus, too much can make us unwell. Signs: headaches, tummy aches, trouble sleeping, irritability.

teach.heading: Healthy coping
bullets: Talk to someone you trust
Exercise, fresh air and sleep
Prayer, dua and Qur'an
Hobbies, art and time with family
teach.note: Show coping strategies. Pair each with a reason it helps. Link to RECIPE Resilience and sabr. Explain unhelpful strategies such as hiding feelings, staying up late, or being unkind to others. Ask: ‘Which strategies work for you?’

teach.heading: Asking for help
bullets: Tell a parent, carer or teacher
Your GP can help with persistent worries
Childline: 0800 1111
Asking for help is a strength
teach.note: Normalise seeking help. Reassure pupils that adults want to help. Remind them that persistent low mood, worry or changes in sleep or appetite deserve attention. If a pupil appears to be at risk of harm, follow the Safeguarding Policy and speak to the DSL immediately.

practice: Sort into helpful or unhelpful ways to cope: (a) talking to a parent (b) staying up all night on a device (c) going for a walk (d) bottling up feelings.
Choose three stressors from our list. Match each with one strategy.
Complete: ‘If I was worried for a long time, I would tell… because…’
independent: Create a ‘Wellbeing toolbox’ with six strategies, including one from our faith.
Write a letter of advice to a younger pupil who is stressed about a test.
Plan a balanced week with time for study, worship, family, play and rest.
exit: Why is mental health as important as physical health?
Name two coping strategies and one person you could ask for help.
lessons.homework: Try two strategies from your toolbox this week and write how each made you feel.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pictorial toolbox and a mood scale. EAL: simplified vocabulary with images. Stretch: design a poster for the school on looking after our minds.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Healthy mind and growing up
lessons.title: Growing up well: hygiene, modesty and caring for my body
objectives: Explain why our bodies need more care as we grow older
Plan a daily hygiene routine linked to taharah
Explain modesty (haya) and privacy, and know who to ask about growing up

keywords.def: a trust: something given to us to look after
keeping your body and clothes clean to stay healthy
purity and cleanliness in Islam
modesty that stops us doing what is wrong or shameful
the right to keep your body and personal things to yourself

starter: Bismillah. Name two ways to look after your mind.
What does 'cleanliness is half of faith' mean to you?
Who is a trusted adult you could ask a question?

teach.heading: Our bodies are an amanah
bullets: Allah created our bodies and gave them to us as a trust
We thank Allah by looking after them
Bodies grow taller and stronger as we get older
Everyone grows at their own pace
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teacher note: this is a PSHE health and hygiene lesson. It does not teach puberty or reproduction: at the Academy, puberty and its fiqh are taught from Year 7, to boys and girls separately, and parents are the first people to talk to their children about growing up. If a pupil asks a detailed question about bodies or puberty, thank them and suggest they ask a parent at home; pass any worrying question to the DSL. Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, 'Your body has a right over you' (Bukhari). Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Cleanliness is half of faith
bullets: Wash or shower every day, and after exercise
Clean clothes, socks and underwear every day
Brush teeth twice a day; the miswak is sunnah
Wash hands before eating and after the toilet
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that purity is half of faith (Muslim). As we grow older we sweat more, so daily washing matters more; some older pupils may choose to use a deodorant. Link to wudu: we already wash our hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet several times a day. The Prophet (peace be upon him) loved the miswak (Bukhari and Muslim). Keep it practical and positive, and never single out a pupil.

teach.heading: My daily routine

head: Time
Habit
Why it helps
rows: Wash face, brush teeth, clean clothes
A fresh start for Fajr and lessons
Removes germs and follows the Sunnah
Wash or shower and change clothes
Removes sweat and keeps skin healthy
Brush teeth, make wudu, say the du'a
Clean teeth and a calm end to the day

teach.note: Build the routine with the class and ask pupils to add one habit of their own. The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that when we go to bed we should make wudu as for prayer and lie on the right side (Bukhari and Muslim, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib).

teach.heading: Haya: modesty and privacy
bullets: Haya is a branch of faith
We dress modestly and cover our bodies
We knock and ask permission before entering a room
Private parts are private: say no, go and tell
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that haya is a branch of faith (Bukhari and Muslim). Link to Qur'an 24:58, which teaches children to ask permission before entering their parents' rooms at certain times. Revisit the body-safety rule from earlier years: no one should touch or look at the parts covered by underwear, or ask you to keep a secret about it; say no, get away and tell a trusted adult. Keep the language calm and simple.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Someone you chat to in a game asks for a photo of you and says, 'Keep this a secret from your parents.' What should you do?
options: Send it, because they are friendly
Do not send it, and tell a trusted adult straight away
Keep the secret but do not reply
Send a photo of someone else instead
check.why: Asking for photos and for secrets from parents are warning signs, so refuse and tell a trusted adult. Keeping the secret leaves the pupil unprotected; sending any photo, of yourself or someone else, is never safe.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Reassure pupils that they will never be in trouble for telling. Remind them of Childline on 0800 1111.

practice: Put in order for a morning routine: brush teeth; wake up and say the du'a; wash face; put on clean clothes.
True or false: (a) We need to wash more as we grow older. (b) Haya means being rude. (c) It is fine to keep a secret that makes you feel worried.
Give two ways we show haya at home.
independent: Design a 'Growing up well' poster with five hygiene habits and one hadith about cleanliness.
Write a daily routine card from morning to bedtime, with a time and a reason for each habit.
Write four sentences explaining what haya means and how it protects us.
exit: Name three hygiene habits you will keep every day.
What should you do if someone asks you to keep a secret that worries you?
lessons.homework: Show your routine card to a parent or carer and ask them for one tip about looking after yourself as you grow up. Write it down.
lessons.send: SEND: picture routine cards and a visual timetable. EAL: key words with images (wash, clean, private, modest). Stretch: find out three facts about the Sunnah of the miswak and present them.
